In mathematics, a '''Pythagorean hodograph curve''' or '''PH curve''' is a [[curve]] defined by a polynomial [[parametric equation]] for which the [[speed]] (the derivative of [[arc length]]) also has a polynomial parametric equation.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|p=V}} This allows the arc length itself to be determined by integrating the speed. Additionally, dividing by the speed gives a rational parameterization of the [[unit normal]] to the curve, and of the [[parallel curve]]s to the given curves. For these reasons, researchers have investigated the use of Pythagorean hodograph curves as [[spline (mathematics)|splines]] in [[geometric design]].

Here, "hodograph" is another word for a [[derivative]].{{sfn|Farouki|2008|page=2}} They are called Pythagorean hodograph curves because their derivatives obey an equation analogous to the equation in the [[Pythagorean theorem]].

==Plane curves==
A [[plane curve]] with polynomial parameterization <math>(x(t),y(t))</math> is a Pythagorean hodograph curve when there exists a polynomial <math>\sigma(t)</math> satisfying the equation of the Pythagorean theorem:{{sfn|Farouki|2008|loc=Equation 17.1|page=382}} <math display=block>\sigma(t)^2=x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2.</math>
Here, <math>\sigma(t)</math> is the speed traveled by a point that takes position <math>(x(t),y(t))</math> at time <math>t</math>.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|page=369}}

===Real characterization===
The curves of this form can be generated by a formula analogous to a formula for generating [[Pythagorean triple]]s. Let <math>u(t)</math>, <math>v(t)</math>, and <math>w(t)</math> be any three polynomials, and set
<math display=block>\begin{align}
x'(t)&=\bigl(u(t)^2-v(t)^2\bigr)w(t)\\
y'(t)&=2u(t)v(t)w(t)\\
\sigma(t)&=\bigl(u(t)^2+v(t)^2\bigr)w(t)\\
\end{align}</math>
Then these three polynomials obey the Pythagorean equation defining a Pythagorean hodograph curve, and the parameterization <math>\bigl(x(t),y(t)\bigr)</math> of the curve itself can be obtained by integrating <math>x'(t)</math> and <math>y'(t)</math>. Every Pythagorean hodograph curve takes this form.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|pages=382–383}}

===Complex characterization===
A simpler alternative formulation of this characterization applies to the ''regular'' Pythagorean hodograph curves, those whose derivative never vanishes over the range of parameters of interest.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|page=133}} It uses the [[complex plane]], in which a curve may be described by a single parametric equation <math>r(t)</math>. In this plane, for every regular polynomial curve <math>r(t)</math>, the curve <math display=block>\hat r(t)=\int r'(t)^2 dt</math> defines a regular Pythagorean hodograph curve, and every regular Pythagorean hodograph curve can be obtained in this way. Because this is an [[indefinite integral]], it can be offset by an arbitrary constant, corresponding to an arbitrary translation of the given curve. Choosing this constant to make the curve start at the [[Origin (mathematics)|origin]] makes the correspondence between regular curves <math>r(t)</math> and regular Pythagorean hodograph curves <math>\hat r(t)</math> into a [[bijection]].{{sfn|Farouki|2008|loc=19.2 One-to-one correspondence|pages=409–413}}

===Examples===
A line, parameterized by choosing <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> to both be linear functions of a parameter <math>t</math>, is automatically a Pythagorean hodograph curve. Its speed is a constant, a degree-zero polynomial.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|page=400}}

There are no quadratic Pythagorean hodograph curves.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|page=400}}

[[File:CubiqueTschirnhausen.svg|thumb|The [[Tschirnhausen cubic]]]]
The simplest nonlinear curves that are Pythagorean hodograph curves are [[cubic curve]]s. Not every cubic curve can be parameterized in this way. The cubic Pythagorean hodograph curves can be described as [[Bézier curve]]s, defined by a sequence of control points <math>u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4</math> for which <math>u_1u_2u_3</math> and <math>u_2u_3u_4</math> are [[similar triangle]]s.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|pages=400–404}} Alternatively, if these points are taken to belong to the [[complex plane]] with the differences between them defined as <math>\Delta_i=u_{i+1}-u_i</math>, then these differences must obey the equation <math>\Delta_1\Delta_3=\Delta_2^2</math>.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|loc=Equation 19.11|page=415}} Every such curve is an arc of a scaled [[Tschirnhausen cubic]], and every arc of the Tschirnhausen cubic is a Pythagorean hodograph curve.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|p=384}}

==Properties==
===Arc length===
The only curve that can be parameterized by [[rational function]]s with constant speed is a line.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|loc=Section 16.1: In search of an elusive ideal|pages=370–374}} In part for this reason, computing the lengths of many types of curve has been difficult, with closed forms known only for certain special curves.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|loc=Section 16.2: The rectification of curves|pages=374–377}} Even as simple a curve as the [[ellipse]] does not have a [[closed-form expression]] for its perimeter, which can instead be expressed as an [[elliptic integral]].{{sfn|Chandrupatla|Osler|2010}} However, for Pythagorean hodograph curves, the arc length may be obtained in closed form by integrating the speed <math>\sigma(t)</math>.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|loc=17.3 Parametric speed and arc length|pages=386–388}}

===Tangents, normals, and offsets===
The unit [[tangent vector]] to a Pythagorean hodograph curve is obtained by dividing the parameterization to the curve by its speed, and the unit [[normal vector]] is obtained by rotating the tangent vector by 90°. This gives a parameterization by [[rational function]]s rather than by polynomials.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|loc=17.4 Differential and integral properties|pages=388–389}} The [[parallel curve]]s of a Pythagorean hodograph curve may be obtained as linear combinations of the parameterizations of the given curve and its normal vector.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|loc=17.5 Rational offsets of PH curves|pages=389–391}}

==Three dimensions==
A three-dimensional [[space curve]] with polynomial parameterization <math>\bigl(x(t),y(t),z(t)\bigr)</math> is a Pythagorean hodograph curve when there exists a polynomial <math>\sigma(t)</math> satisfying the equation:{{sfn|Farouki|2008|loc=Equation 21.1|page=455}} <math display=block>\sigma(t)^2=x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2+z'(t)^2.</math>
These curves can be generated from polynomials over the [[quaternion]]s analogously to the way plane Pythagorean hodograph curves can be generated from [[complex polynomial]]s.{{sfn|Farouki|2008|page=455}}
